questions.story: 9:25 AM — An employee opened an unexpected .zip file from a shipping contact, and the computer displayed a strange security warning.
questions.question: What is the first thing you must do to contain the potentially compromised device?
options: Restart the computer to see if the warning goes away.
Immediately disconnect the device from Wi-Fi/Ethernet to stop potential malware from spreading or communicating externally.
Email the supplier back asking if the file was safe.
Copy all business files onto an unformatted USB flash drive.
questions.feedback: Disconnecting the device limits potential communication with an attacker and reduces the opportunity for the incident to spread to other systems.

questions.story: 9:35 AM — The device is isolated from the internet. You need to handle internal and external communication.
questions.question: How should you escalate this incident?
options: Inform relevant staff not to open emails from that supplier and report the suspicious email/header/domain to your IT support or email provider.
Hide the incident from the rest of the team to avoid panic.
Call the supplier and demand they pay for a new laptop.
Reply to the suspicious email warning the attacker that you called the police.
questions.feedback: Internal notification helps prevent other employees from opening the same attachment, while reporting the suspicious email can help the organization identify and block similar messages.

questions.story: 10:00 AM — The infected device has been disconnected and analyzed.
questions.question: What is the proper recovery step before bringing the device back online?
options: Reconnect to Wi-Fi immediately if no further pop-ups appear.
Run a full antivirus scan, remove flagged malicious files, and verify system integrity or restore from a clean backup.
Delete the .zip file from the Downloads folder and resume work.
questions.feedback: Removing the downloaded file alone does not establish that the device is clean. The system should be checked and, where necessary, restored from a known-clean state before reconnection.

questions.story: 10:20 AM — The device has been scanned and restored using the appropriate recovery process.
questions.question: What should you verify before returning the device to normal business use?
options: Reconnect it immediately because the suspicious file has been removed.
Confirm that security controls are functioning, review relevant account activity, and document the incident and recovery actions.
Delete the incident records to prevent unnecessary concern.
Give the recovered device to another employee without informing them.
questions.feedback: Verification helps confirm that the device is properly secured before normal use resumes, while documentation preserves the incident record and recovery actions.
